item.title: Functional stratification of YWHAZ variants explains distinct neurodevelopmental disorders.
item.author: Popov IK, Motta M, Prandi IG, Tao J, Priolo M, Ferilli M, Jamra RA, Balton EV, Banneau G, Bruselles A, Bukele K, Chapel-Crespo C, Chillemi G, Ciolfi A, Cordeddu V, Crunk A, Daniele P, De Luca A, Doco-Fenzy M, Elias ER, Flex E, Gangaram B, Gasperian K, Grand K, Holder D, Julia S, Klee E, Keren B, Leoni C, Leppig KA, Mancini C, Marica M, Micule I, Onesimo R, Polster T, Radio FC, Abdul-Rahman OA, Rauch A, Schimmenti LA, Schrier Vergano SA, Szialta C, Tenney J, Terrusa M, Weaver KN, William N, Yoon G, Zampino G, Chang C, Tartaglia M.
item.description:
The application of clinical genomics in personalized medical practice increasingly reveals that variants from single loci can lead to phenotypic heterogeneity. This necessitates functional characterization and classification of serial variants to correlate their associated clinical features and molecular properties. Recently, a few putative pathogenic variants in YWHAZ, encoding the 14-3-3ζ protein, have been implicated in clinically variable isolated and syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotypes, based on a few reported affected individuals, but the molecular basis of this heterogeneity has remained unclear. item.title: De novo variants in the essential splicing factor gene SRSF3 cause variable developmental phenotypes.
item.author: Lisfeld J, Chinn IK, Yuan B, Casar C, Müller C, Elron E, Zaks Hoffer G, Orenstein N, Tveten K, Delanne J, Safraou H, Denommé-Pichon AS, Aref-Eshghi E, Robin NH, Rothrock ED, Wentzensen IM, Messer GJ, Schnur RE, Rabin R, Lewis S, Sleutels F, Kant SG, Lupski JR, Kutsche K, Harms FL.
item.description:
SRSF3 (SRp20), a member of the serine/arginine-rich protein family of splicing factors, plays a central role in constitutive and alternative splicing. The C-terminal arginine/serine-rich domain of SRSF3 undergoes dynamic phosphorylation cycles that regulate its subcellular localization, protein-protein interactions, and nuclear mRNA export while also indirectly modulating the RNA-binding capability. We report nine individuals with variable developmental phenotypes, including developmental delay and/or mild to moderate intellectual disability as the most consistent feature, and de novo SRSF3 variants. item.title: The genetic architecture of pentanucleotide repeat variation and disease association.
item.author: Xu IRL, Pellerin D, Van De Vondel L, Weisburd B, Dolzhenko E, Danzi MC, Zuchner S.
item.description:
Pentanucleotide tandem repeats (PNTRs) are associated with at least eleven neurological disorders in which pathogenic alleles are defined by both large repeat expansions and disease-specific non-reference motifs. However, population-scale, sequence-resolved datasets of PNTR variation have not been available, limiting interpretation of repeat alleles identified through long-read sequencing. Here, we genotyped 47,952 PNTR loci in 543 high-coverage PacBio HiFi genomes spanning five ancestry superpopulations, with validation in 500 Oxford Nanopore genomes. Using base-pair-resolved decomposition, we generated a genome-wide reference of PNTR length and sequence variation. Disease-associated PNTR loci emerged as extreme outliers for repeat-length variability, extreme allele length, and motif diversity. item.title: Accurate detection of sub-1% frequency somatic mutations by whole-genome sequencing.
item.author: Jang Y, Gardiner S, Wang Y, Natu A, Dehankar MK, Tomasini L, Panda A, Cibulskis C, Anderson L, Coorens THH, Oh JW, Urban AE, Ardlie K, Marth G, Vaccarino FM, Abyzov A.
item.description:
Continuous advances in read accuracy have positioned bulk whole-genome sequencing as a promising approach for somatic mutation discovery in research and clinical settings, but its utility for detecting low-frequency mutations in high-coverage data has not been thoroughly assessed. We utilized an experimental design featuring (1) primary human fibroblasts with naturally occurring mutations and expanded subclonal populations, (2) induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines corresponding to subclones, and (3) additional iPSC lines originating from other fibroblasts from the same donor, enabling comprehensive evaluation of mutation detection across analytical methods and sequencing depths. item.title: De novo MAP2K4 variants cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome and impaired JNK signaling in iPSC-derived neurons.
item.author: Nomakuchi TT, Rippert AL, Santos De León SA, Gonzalez EM, Li D, Angireddy R, Finoti LS, Faletra F, Musante L, Tuula R, Amor DJ, von Wintzingerode L, Jamra RA, Stover SR, Buchan JG, Hayek J, Leon E, Attie-Bitach T, Rio M, Baujat G, Wallach E, Smail A, Dias KR, Pfeifer U, Peterson A, Ahrens-Nicklas RC, Bhoj EJK.
item.description:
MAP2K4 encodes a kinase that activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway, which is essential for human neurodevelopment. While somatic MAP2K4 loss has been observed in cancer, germline variants have not previously been linked to human disease. We describe nine individuals with de novo MAP2K4 variants and one individual with a MAP2K4 variant of unknown inheritance who present with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. Shared features include developmental delay or intellectual disability, epilepsy, and variable congenital malformations, most commonly affecting the genitourinary system. To define the mechanism, we generated CRISPR-edited induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons with MAP2K4 deficiency. item.title: Large-scale integration of functional assay data for the resolution of germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants of uncertain significance.
item.author: Lyra PCM, Brito S, Parsons M, Hu C, Nepomuceno TC, Nguyen NP, Dalcolmo L, Richardson ME, de Oliveira G, da Silva J, Caleca L, Huang H, Sahu S, Bose M, Rossing M, Dace P, Findlay GM, Villani R, Hazra A, Martins A, Caputo SM, Millot GA, Yuen Yie JN, Carvalho MA, Cline MS, Radice P, Mesman RLS, Zampiga V, Joseph V, Nathanson KL, Michailidou K, Iversen ES, Sharan S, Spurdle AB, Vreeswijk MPG, Couch FJ, Monteiro ANA, ENIGMA Consortium.
item.description:
Carriers of BRCA1 and BRCA2 pathogenic variants are at a significantly elevated risk for several cancers. Widespread germline genetic testing has led to a significant increase in the detection of variants of uncertain significance (VUSs) in these genes. To assess variant pathogenicity, we curated, harmonized, and integrated functional data for 3,247 BRCA1 and 6,177 BRCA2 missense variants derived from BRCA1/2 functional assays. Functional results were harmonized across studies by converting data into ordinal categorical variables. We applied ClinGen variant interpretation guidelines for each assay to assign evidence for or against pathogenicity. item.title: Loss of the human BRIP1 C terminus does not cause Fanconi anemia.
item.author: Droste A, Sobeck A, Knaup J, Popp I, Vodopiutz J, Janecke AR, Fiebig B, Maringa M, Faust U, Carter N, Maiwald R, Kager L, Hauke J, Schindler D, Hark R, Lalomia V, Kulka R, Kratz CP, Repczynska A, Kalb R.
item.description:
Fanconi anemia (FA) is a genetic disorder characterized by congenital anomalies, progressive bone marrow failure, and an increased cancer risk. FA patient cells are hypersensitive to DNA interstrand crosslinks (ICLs), which cause chromosomal and genomic instability if left unrepaired. We identified 11 individuals from seven families who are homozygous for one of two C-terminally truncating variants in BRIP1 (previously known as FANCJ), c.2947del (p.Ile983Leufs ∗ 2) (n = 3) or c.2992_2995del (p.Lys998Glufs ∗ 60) (n = 8). None of them exhibited hematologic manifestations of FA, including bone marrow failure, myelodysplasia, or any FA-associated early-onset cancer types. Patient-derived blood cells showed stable levels of the BRIP1 p.Ile983Leufs ∗ 2 variant and were resistant to ICL-inducing agents. item.title: A massively parallel reporter assay of MECP2cis-regulatory elements reveals genetic candidates for male-biased autism.
item.author: Meyer-Schuman R, Cherry F, Sui Y, Papastathopoulos-Katsaros A, Zhong Y, Li Y, Wang T, Hennick K, Karunakaran D, Berk-Rauch H, Liu Z, Chakravarti A, Nowakowski T, Eichler EE, Zoghbi H.
item.description:
Autism affects male individuals four times more often than female individuals, yet the basis of this sex bias remains unclear. One hypothesis is that this sex bias is due to genetic variants in X chromosome genes where haploinsufficiency causes neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). In heterozygous XX female probands, a complete loss-of-function variant in one of these genes often causes syndromic NDD, but the same variant is too deleterious for survival in hemizygous XY males. A mild hypomorphic variant, however, may be tolerated in a female carrier but may produce milder neurological phenotypes in a male proband. item.title: Hypomorphic IDUA genotypes are associated with retinitis pigmentosa in individuals without syndromic mucopolysaccharidosis type I.
item.author: Lin S, Yu SH, Browning AC, Sangermano R, Poplawski AB, Stepien KM, Kiraly P, Ridgeway AR, Rump P, Karali M, Simonelli F, Finnegan LK, Farrar GJ, Chadderton N, Kenna PF, Duignan E, McCance E, Fischer MD, Lachmann R, Finezilber Y, Leo SM, Robson AG, Guha N, Murphy E, Sperring S, Rodenburg K, Jestin A, Haer-Wigman L, Pott JWR, Habing MMB, Place EM, Huckfeldt RM, Banfi S, Votruba M, Bujakowska KM, Flanagan-Steet H, Mahroo OA, Webster AR, Roosing S, Steet R, Arno G.
item.description:
Bi-allelic variants in IDUA classically cause mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I), a multisystem lysosomal storage disorder. This study describes 14 individuals from 12 families presenting with retinitis pigmentosa, later attributed to bi-allelic IDUA genotypes. Notably, seven individuals, despite comprehensive systemic assessments, showed no features consistent with MPS I at last assessment (aged 46-73 years). Leukocyte α-L-iduronidase activity was reduced but not abolished across all individuals assessed (n = 9), supporting a shared mechanistic basis for the mild, retina-predominant, or exclusively retinal phenotype. No individual carried bi-allelic null genotypes; most had a loss-of-function allele paired with a missense variant, consistent with an overall hypomorphic genotype.
